title: Mitigation of harmful algal blooms using modified clays: Theory, mechanisms, and applications
authors: Zhiming Yu, Xiuxian Song, Xihua Cao, Yang Liu
scale: Review of lab and field use; China field applications
result: Surface-modified clays remove HAB cells with efficiencies up to hundreds of times those of natural clays at 4-10 t/km2; the most widely used field HAB mitigation method in China.
env_effects: Authors conclude lab and field results show modified clay improves water quality and has no negative effects on aquatic ecosystems; the clay settles to the seabed and is not retrieved.

title: Controlling Harmful Algal Blooms Through Clay Flocculation1
authors: Mario R. Sengco, Donald Mark Anderson
organism: Karenia brevis, Heterosigma akashiwo, Pfiesteria piscicida, Aureococcus anophagefferens, Cochlodinium
scale: Review of lab, mesocosm, field-enclosure and flume work; field use in Japan and Korea
dose: Lab/mesocosm 0.10-4 g/L clay (0.25-0.5 g/L in the scaled tests), some with PAC; field: Japan montmorillonite/kaolinite 1.3-400 g/m2 (200 g/m2 near fish pens); South Korea 1996 ~60,000 t yellow loess over 260 km2 at 400 g/m2
result: Scale-up table: K. brevis removal 97% in lab (0.5 g/L) and 90% in settling columns (0.25 g/L); Heterocapsa triquetra 85% (Texas mesocosms), 68% (Florida mesocosms), and 100%, 89% and 41% in a flume at 3, 10 and 20 cm/s (0.25 g/L). In Korea, C. polykrikoides removal was calculated at 90-99% to 2 m depth and fisheries losses fell from $100 million to $1 million in the first year.
env_effects: Turbidity returned near background within ~4 h. Phosphatic clay with or without PAC was not lethal to four benthic species (amphipods, sheepshead minnow, grass shrimp) in 4-28 d tests, and settled clay/K. brevis flocs were no more toxic than K. brevis alone. Juvenile hard clams: no mortality, no growth effect when flocs settled, but ~90% lower shell and tissue growth when clay stayed resuspended at 0.25 g/L for two weeks. PAC made settled flocs more erodible. Extracellular brevetoxins were removed by up to 70%; cell mortality rose with clay dose and time in the settled layer.
key_details: Symposium review (Sengco & Anderson) summarizing US lab, mesocosm, limnocorral and flume work plus Japanese and Korean field use. Removal efficiency fell as scale and flow increased (97% lab to 68% in Florida mesocosms and 41% in a 20 cm/s flume). Korean field removal numbers (90-99%) and the $100M to $1M loss reduction are secondhand reports without controls. Benthic tests found no acute toxicity from clay itself, but prolonged resuspension cut clam growth ~90%. Several cited results were unpublished or in press at the time.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '>80% removal' hides the drop with scale and flow (68% in Florida mesocosms, 41% in the fastest flume) and omits the ~90% clam growth reduction under resuspended clay.

title: Removal of red- and brown-tide cells using clay flocculation. I. Laboratory culture experiments with Gymnodinium breve and Aureococcus anophagefferens
authors: MR Sengco, A Li, Kimberly I. Tugend, D. M. Kulis, D. M. Anderson
scale: Triplicate borosilicate test tubes; 25 US clays + Korean loess
duration: 2.5 h removal tests under quiescent conditions; viability/recovery followed over days
result: Twelve clays removed >90% of G. breve at 0.25 g/L (phosphatic clay up to 80% at 0.04 g/L), but no clay exceeded 40% removal of A. anophagefferens at 0.25 g/L unless dispersed through the culture (80%); alum, PAC and organic flocculants alone removed only 30-50%.
env_effects: G. breve fully recovered at clay <0.03 g/L (growth delayed 24 h); mortality up to 100% with no recovery at ≥0.50 g/L; mortality near zero after 2.5 h contact but rose significantly after 12 h.
key_details: Lab screening of 26 clays against G. breve (CCMP 718) and A. anophagefferens (BP3B) in triplicate tubes, removal measured by in vivo fluorescence after 2.5 h versus clay-free controls corrected for sinking. Twelve clays (mostly montmorillonite, bentonite, Florida phosphatic clay) removed >90% of G. breve at 0.25 g/L; IMC-P2 phosphatic clay reached 80% at 0.04 g/L. No clay removed >40% of A. anophagefferens at 0.25 g/L unless dispersed through the culture (then 80%). Alum, PAC and organic flocculants alone removed only 30-50%, but 5 ppm PAC cut the clay needed for G. breve by an order of magnitude. Removed cells can survive and regrow at low loadings, so removal is not always kill.

title: Exposure of blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) to modified clay treatment of Karenia brevis as a bloom control strategy
authors: Victoria M. Devillier, Emily R. Hall, Donald Mark Anderson, Kristy A. Lewis
scale: 48 adult blue crabs in individual 20 L static tanks; 4 treatments (seawater, clay only, K. brevis only, clay-treated K. brevis), n = 12 tanks per treatment
dose: Modified Clay II (PAC-modified) 0.5 g/L, sprayed on the surface (authors note 0.1 g/L already removes cells); K. brevis 1 × 10⁶ cells/L; re-dosed on day 4 after a full water change
result: Clay cut K. brevis cells in the water column by 95% at 24 h and 98% at 48 h, but total brevetoxin in the water did not differ from untreated K. brevis tanks. Crab deaths were 2 (seawater), 1 (clay), 1 (K. brevis), 0 (clay + K. brevis), with no significant differences in survival or reflexes.
env_effects: Clay dropped tank pH to 7.25 vs 7.86 in seawater on day 1, recovering within 72 h. Water-column brevetoxin was not reduced by clay. No detectable effect on adult crab survival or reflexes, though K. brevis alone killed only 1 of 12 crabs, so power to detect harm or benefit was low.
key_details: Randomised tank experiment: 48 adult blue crabs, one per 20 L static tank, 12 tanks per treatment. Clay (Modified Clay II, 0.5 g/L) and K. brevis (10⁶ cells/L) were dosed twice, on days 0 and 4, over 8 days. Cell removal was 95% at 24 h and 98% at 48 h (removal efficiency vs untreated 93% at 24 h). Total water-column brevetoxins did not differ between clay-treated and untreated K. brevis tanks at any time (GLM p > 0.05). Only 4 of 48 crabs died, none in the first 48 h, and survival (Cox model) and reflexes did not differ. Clay lowered pH for ~72 h.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record left out that clay did not reduce dissolved/total brevetoxin in the water and caused a transient pH drop (7.25 vs 7.86). It also missed that the untreated K. brevis arm barely harmed crabs (1/12 died), so the 'no harm' result has low power.

title: Mesocosm study of PAC-modified clay effects on Karenia brevis cells and toxins, chemical dynamics, and benthic invertebrate physiology
authors: Victoria M. Devillier, Emily R. Hall, Vince Lovko, Richard H. Pierce, Donald Mark Anderson, Kristy A. Lewis
organism: Karenia brevis; blue crab, sea urchin, hard clam
scale: Twelve 1400 L indoor mesocosm tanks (Mote Marine Lab, Sarasota, April 2022), 4 treatments x 3 tanks: seawater only, MC II only, K. brevis only, K. brevis + MC II; each tank with 12 hard clams, 6 sea urchins, 2 blue crabs
dose: MC II (PAC-modified kaolinite) 0.2 g/L vs 1e6 cells/L
result: Cell removal was 57% after 8 h and 95% after 48 h; some brevetoxin analogs (BTx-3, BTx-B5) were higher in treated tanks and in the floc.
env_effects: Dissolved P significantly lower in MC II tanks after 2 h; DIC and alkalinity reduced, pCO2 higher (MC II only) at 2 h; turbidity back to control by 48 h. No lethal or sublethal differences in clams, urchins or crabs vs untreated K. brevis within 72 h. Some brevetoxin analogs (BTx-3, BTx-B5) higher in treated water and floc.
key_details: Randomised mesocosm experiment: K. brevis (CCMP 2228) at 1 × 10⁶ cells/L sprayed with MC II (PAC-modified kaolinite) slurry at 0.2 g/L, with wavemaker circulation (~26 cm/s), static (no recirculation) for 72 h, n = 3 tanks per treatment. Cell removal was 57% at 8 h and 95% at 48 h, slightly lower than earlier lab work; authors suggest flow (>10 cm/s) reduces particle-collision removal. BTx-1 and BTx-2 were higher in untreated water at 24-48 h, but toxin removal was less than expected. Animal endpoints (mortality, physiology) showed no MC II effect over 72 h; longer exposure not tested.

title: Degradation of paralytic shellfish toxins during flocculation of Alexandrium pacificum by an oxidized modified clay: A laboratory experiment
authors: Weijia Song, Xiuxian Song, Hui‐Hui Shen, Yu Ding, Ruihong Cheng, Zhiming Yu
scale: 1 L glass cylinders, 2000 cells/mL A. pacificum (strain ATHK), 4 treatments + control in triplicate
dose: PMPS-MC (kaolin:potassium peroxymonosulfate 20:1 by mass) at 5 and 10 mg/L expressed as PMPS content; PMPS alone at 5 and 10 mg/L as comparison
result: PMPS-MC removed >95% of cells from the water column within 3 h and kept it low for 48 h; extracellular PSTs fell below detection within 15 min and total toxin content fell 56-73% within 15 min. Over 70% of cells turned into pellicle cysts within 3 h.
env_effects: Viable cells in the flocculated sediment continued to secrete toxins; clay transformed toxins to less toxic analogues.
key_details: Lab cylinder experiment (triplicate) comparing oxidant PMPS alone with PMPS-modified kaolin at 5 and 10 mg/L PMPS, sampled at 0, 15 min, 3, 9, 24 and 48 h against an untreated control. Water-column removal exceeded 95% at 3 h for both PMPS-MC doses; PMPS alone removed slightly less and low-dose PMPS let the water-column density rise again within 48 h. Toxin profile shifted from GTX1/4 toward less toxic GTX2/3 and C1/2. Caveat: many treated cells formed pellicle cysts and some viable cells in the floc kept releasing toxin, so removal is not complete kill.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record dose '10 mg/L' is the PMPS (oxidant) content, not the clay loading; with the 20:1 kaolin:PMPS ratio the clay itself is about 20 times higher. Record omits the >95% cell removal and the pellicle-cyst formation.

title: Removal of cyanobacterial blooms in Taihu Lake using local soils. I. Equilibrium and kinetic screening on the flocculation of Microcystis aeruginosa using commercially available clays and minerals
authors: Gang Pan, Mingming Zhang, Hao Chen, Hua Zou, Hai Yan
scale: Jar flocculation tests; 26 clays/minerals; cultured M. aeruginosa (FACHB) resuspended in 0.5% NaCl at 4.86 × 10⁹ cells/L
result: At 0.7 g/L, Type I materials (sepiolite, talc, ferric oxide, kaolinite) had Q8h > 90% with t50 < 15 min; 14 Type III clays had Q8h < 50% (no practical value). At 0.2 g/L all materials fell below 60% except sepiolite (~97%).
env_effects: Not assessed in the abstract; the clay-algae floc is left in the lake sediment.
key_details: Lab screening of 26 commercially available clays and minerals (<90 µm) against a lab culture of M. aeruginosa, removal tracked by chlorophyll a over 8 h, when curves reached equilibrium. Table 2 lists 8-h removal at 0.7 g/L: talc 97.6%, ferric oxide 96.5%, sepiolite I 96.3%, ferroferric oxide 95.0%, kaolinite 93.9%, argillaceous rocks 92.6%, down to ~29% for pumice/scoria; Ca-bentonite only 34.7%. Sepiolite's performance at low dose was attributed to netting and bridging. Cells were harvested and resuspended in saline, not natural lake water, and replication is not stated in the sections read.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '4 of 26 removed >90%' follows the abstract's Type I grouping; Table 2 actually shows 6 materials above 90% at 0.7 g/L (incl. ferroferric oxide 95.0% and argillaceous rocks 92.6%), grouped also by removal rate.

title: ‘Floc and Sink’ Technique Removes Cyanobacteria and Microcystins from Tropical Reservoir Water
authors: Renan Silva Arruda, Natália Pessoa Noyma, Leonardo de Magalhães, Marcella Coelho Berjante Mesquita, Éryka Costa de Almeida, Ernani Pinto et al.
scale: Test tubes and 1 L cylinders with tropical reservoir bloom water
dose: PAC (best dose 3 mg/L) + lanthanum-modified bentonite and/or local red soil
result: PAC plus ballast removed 97 +/- 1.8% of chlorophyll-a from the top of the water column (20-60x lower than controls), 4.3-7.5x more biomass than other treatments; PAC alone did not sink the biomass.
env_effects: PAC alone raised extracellular microcystin 3.5-6x; with ballast the bottom layer had extracellular MC up to 8x above controls, so toxin moves to the sediment layer; PAC lowered pH and PSII efficiency.

title: Post-ecological effect and risk assessment of using modified clay in harmful algal bloom mitigation: An attempt based on the responses of zooplankton Brachionus plicatilis and bivalve Mytilus edulis
authors: Sai Cao, Zhengyu Liu, Bin Zhou, Yongshun Jiang, Mengxue Xu, You Wang
organism: Karenia mikimotoi; rotifer Brachionus plicatilis; blue mussel Mytilus edulis
scale: Removal test in triplicate colorimetric tubes; rotifer test in 24-well plates (10 larvae/well, triplicate, 4 groups); mussel test in 14 L tanks, 30 M. edulis per concentration, one tank per treatment
dose: PAC-modified kaolin 0.1 g/L for removal and rotifer tests; 0, 0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 g/L for mussels (0.1 g/L stated as the field application concentration)
duration: 2 h settling for removal; rotifer life-table over days (~180 h); mussel exposure with clay held in suspension
result: Modified clay at 0.1 g/L removed 81% of K. mikimotoi with little impact on rotifers or mussels.
env_effects: Rotifers: clay-treated Karenia supernatant did not worsen Karenia-induced growth/reproduction effects within 2 h and survival/reproduction improved by 2 d. Mussels: gill and digestive-gland damage, and changes in filtration rate, digestive enzymes, condition index and mortality at 0.5 and 1.0 g/L; little impact at 0.1 g/L.
key_details: Removal of K. mikimotoi (1.5 × 10⁵ cells/mL) by 0.1 g/L PAC-modified clay was 81 ± 2.3% after 2 h standing (triplicate). Rotifer groups were control, clay-only supernatant, Karenia, and clay-treated Karenia supernatant. The mussel system contained clay and mussels only (no Karenia) at 0-1.0 g/L, with one 10 L tank of 30 mussels per concentration, so tank-level replication is n = 1. AOP and integrated biomarker analyses flagged risk only at 0.5 and 1.0 g/L. Rotifers in the clay-only group began dying earlier (78 h) than controls (122 h).
fulltext_discrepancy: Mussel experiment did not include K. mikimotoi and had one tank per dose (pseudoreplication); 'little impact' applies to 0.1 g/L only.

title: Effect of yellow loess on clearance rate in seven species of benthic, filter-feeding invertebrates
authors: Sandra E. Shumway, Dana M. Frank, Lisa M Ewart, J. Evan Ward
organism: Filter feeders: Crassostrea virginica, C. gigas, Mytilus edulis, M. trossulus, Argopecten irradians, Crepidula fornicata, Obelia hydroid
scale: Lab clearance (depletion) trials at UConn Avery Point (1999), Friday Harbor WA (2000) and Southampton NY (2000); Rhodomonas lens 2.5 × 10⁴ cells/mL as food; hydroid polyp opening by video (20 polyps per treatment)
result: All species were negatively affected. Bay scallops were most sensitive (significant clearance drop at 10 mg/L, 1 g/L and 10 g/L; 100 mg/L not significant, p = 0.076); Obelia polyps closed longer from 10 mg/L; mussels, both oysters and Crepidula were affected only at ≥1 g/L.
env_effects: Direct non-target harm: loess significantly impairs feeding of benthic filter-feeding shellfish (scallops most sensitive) and hydroid behaviour.
key_details: Seven benthic suspension feeders were exposed to five loess concentrations (0.01-10 g/L) at 14-18°C and 28-32 ppt, with algae-only controls; pure loess suspensions caused little to no feeding, so Rhodomonas was added. Analysed with one-way ANOVA and Dunnett tests (nested ANOVA for hydroids). Pseudofaeces were seen in all bivalves at ≥0.01 g/L but not quantified. Authors conclude clay use against HABs 'should be approached with extreme caution'. Short-term feeding trials only; no growth or mortality endpoints and no HAB cells present.

title: Application of clay minerals to remove extracellular ichthyotoxins produced by the dinoflagellates Karlodinium veneficum and Karenia mikimotoi
scale: Rainbow trout gill cell line (RTgill-W1) assay
dose: Loess, zeolite 0-0.5 g/L; PAC 0-0.1 g/L; PAC-modified clays 0-0.25 g/L; bentonites
result: Korean loess, zeolite, PAC and PAC-modified clays did not significantly reduce ichthyotoxicity, whereas high-swelling bentonites removed 100% of toxicity at 0.1 g/L.
env_effects: Efficacy is highly clay- and species-specific; the commonly used loess and PAC-modified clays failed to detoxify.

title: Toxic Alexandrium Treatment in Western Australia: Investigating the Efficacy of Modified Nano Clay
authors: Cherono Sheilah Kwambai, Houda Ennaceri, Alan John Lymbery, Damian W. Laird, Jeffrey J. Cosgrove, Navid Reza Moheimani
scale: Review of lab studies and management options (Western Australia focus)
dose: Modified clays roughly 0.1-2 g/L in reviewed studies
result: Reviewed lab trials report ~75-99% removal of Alexandrium with PAC-modified kaolinite depending on dose (0.2-1 g/L), but the authors note limited scalability to blooms spanning hundreds of km2.
env_effects: Reviewed data show cyst formation rose with clay concentration (17.9-24.6%) while germination fell; recommends coupling treatment with monitoring rather than relying on it.
